title: Digitalizar tienda de abarrotes con el celular — Guía | Treinta
summary: Aprende a digitalizar tu tienda de abarrotes con el celular en 7 días: ahorra tiempo, controla inventario y recupera ventas. Comienza hoy y mejora tu gestión.
body_text: Digitalizar no significa comprar una computadora, contratar a alguien de sistemas ni cambiar todo de golpe. Para una tienda de abarrotes, digitalizar significa pasar del cuaderno al celular, del "me parece que quedan diez" al número exacto en pantalla, y del fiado sin registro al historial claro de quién debe cuánto desde cuándo. Ese cambio toma días, no semanas, y no requiere inversión en equipo ni conocimientos técnicos. En esta guía encontrarás por dónde empezar, en qué orden avanzar y qué herramientas usar para que el proceso no interrumpa la operación diaria del negocio. Por dónde empezar sin detener el negocio El error más común al digitalizar una tienda de abarrotes es querer hacerlo todo al mismo tiempo. Cargar 500 productos al sistema, configurar pagos digitales y capacitar empleados en la misma semana garantiza que nada quede funcionando bien. El método que funciona va en fases. La primera fase es el registro de ventas y caja. Antes de tocar el inventario o los pagos, necesitas que cada peso que entra y sale quede anotado en tiempo real. Registrar cada venta cuando ocurre, cada gasto cuando se paga y el fondo de caja al abrir y cerrar. Con ese hábito instalado, el cierre del día deja de ser un misterio y la caja cuadra porque hay datos que respaldan cada movimiento. La segunda fase es el inventario de los productos principales. No todos los 400 o 500 productos que puede manejar una tienda, sino los 30 o 40 que generan el 70% de las ventas. Cargando esos primeros, el sistema ya descuenta automáticamente cada vez que vendes y te avisa cuando alguno baja del mínimo que defines. La tercera fase son los pagos digitales y el catálogo. Una vez que el registro de ventas y el inventario básico están funcionando, agregar CoDi para cobrar sin comisiones y armar un catálogo para WhatsApp amplía el negocio sin cambiar su operación central. En Treinta puedes ejecutar el registro de ventas y el control de inventario desde un solo celular, sin necesidad de equipo adicional ni de parar la tienda para configurar. ¿Ya usas Treinta? Descarga la app y empieza la primera fase hoy. Inventario digital sin cerrar la tienda El inventario digital no requiere contar todo en un día. Funciona mejor si lo construyes en bloques mientras el negocio opera. El método más práctico es dividir la tienda en zonas y cargar una por día en los momentos de menos tráfico: bebidas el lunes, lácteos el martes, abarrotes secos el miércoles, higiene el jueves. En cuatro días tienes el inventario inicial de los productos principales sin cerrar ni una hora. Para cada producto necesitas solo cuatro datos: nombre, cantidad actual, precio de costo y precio de venta. Con eso el sistema ya puede calcular tu margen por producto y alertarte cuando el stock baje del mínimo que defines. El beneficio aparece desde la primera semana. El dueño de una tienda que empieza a registrar inventario digitalmente deja de hacer pedidos "por si acaso" y empieza a pedir al proveedor exactamente lo que necesita. Eso reduce el capital atrapado en mercancía que no rota y libera efectivo para mejores compras. El software de control de inventarios de Treinta permite cargar productos, registrar entradas y salidas y configurar alertas de stock mínimo desde el celular. Pagos digitales sin terminal ni comisión Agregar pagos digitales a una tienda de abarrotes ya no requiere contratar una terminal ni pagar comisiones mensuales. CoDi, la plataforma de Banxico, permite cobrar mediante código QR directamente desde la app bancaria, sin costo para quien cobra ni para quien paga. La activación toma menos de cinco minutos desde la app del banco. Una vez activa, tienes dos opciones: generar un QR por el monto exacto de cada venta, o imprimir un QR fijo con monto abierto y colocarlo junto a la caja. La segunda opción es más práctica en tiendas con mucho movimiento porque el cliente escanea, ingresa el monto y paga sin que el dueño tenga que sacar el celular en cada transacción. El dinero llega en segundos a la cuenta bancaria, disponible de inmediato. El único requisito es que el cliente tenga CoDi activo en su propia app bancaria, algo que cada vez más personas tienen configurado. Para quienes no lo tienen, la CLABE para transferencia SPEI cubre el resto de los casos. Para que los pagos digitales no generen descuadres de caja, cada cobro QR necesita quedar registrado como venta en el momento en que llega la notificación. El registro de ventas y gastos de Treinta permite hacerlo en segundos con el método de pago desglosado. Catálogo en línea y control de fiados: los dos pasos que más crecimiento generan Un catálogo digital con foto y precio de los productos principales abre una ventana de ventas que funciona cuando la tienda está cerrada. El cliente ve el catálogo en WhatsApp, elige lo que quiere, paga con QR o transferencia y pasa a recoger, sin que hayas hecho una sola llamada. Armar ese catálogo con los 30 o 40 productos de mayor demanda toma una tarde. Las fotos se toman con el mismo celular con luz natural y fondo limpio. El precio y la descripción se cargan en la app. El enlace se comparte en grupos de vecinos o directamente con clientes frecuentes. Esa inversión de una tarde puede generar pedidos recurrentes que antes no existían. El control de fiados es el otro cambio que más impacto tiene en la rentabilidad. Cuando los créditos a clientes se registran digitalmente con nombre, monto y fecha de pago, la tasa de recuperación sube porque el seguimiento es automático. La función de control de deudas de Treinta permite registrar cada fiado desde el celular y ver en cualquier momento cuánto te deben en total y quién tiene más tiempo sin pagar. Los reportes y estadísticas de Treinta consolidan todo: ventas del día, gastos, inventario y fiados pendientes. Ese panorama completo, disponible en el celular en cualquier momento, es lo que convierte a una tienda que opera de memoria en una que toma decisiones con información. Conoce todas las funcionalidades en treinta.co/mx . Empieza hoy con la primera fase: registra ventas y caja. Preguntas frecuentes sobre cómo digitalizar una tienda de abarrotes con el celular ¿Necesito internet todo el día para que funcione la app? Treinta requiere conexión a internet activa para funcionar correctamente. Asegúrate de contar con datos móviles o WiFi estable durante la operación de tu tienda para registrar ventas, actualizar inventario y sincronizar información en tiempo real. ¿Cuánto tiempo toma ver resultados después de digitalizar? El control de caja mejora desde el primer día. El inventario empieza a dar beneficios en la segunda semana cuando ya tienes datos de rotación. Los pedidos por catálogo pueden tardar dos o tres semanas en generar volumen regular. ¿Qué hago si mis empleados no saben usar el celular? Empieza tú solo con el registro de ventas durante las primeras dos semanas. Una vez que el flujo está claro, capacita a cada empleado en una sola función: registrar la venta al cobrar. No intentes que aprendan todo al mismo tiempo. ¿Puedo digitalizar si tengo más de 500 productos? Sí, pero empieza con los 40 o 50 de mayor rotación. Agregar el resto de forma gradual, 20 o 30 por semana, es más sostenible que intentar cargar todo el catálogo de golpe. ¿Qué pasa con los fiados que ya tengo sin registro? title: Jeep Wrangler Buying Guide: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Buy
summary: Discover the ultimate buying guide for purchasing a used Jeep Wrangler, covering every generation since 1986. Whether you're a first-time buyer or a Wrangler enthusiast, this comprehensive overview will help you research your next pre-owned Jeep Wrangler.
body_text: The Wrangler is an iconic vehicle that defines the Jeep brand with its reputation for stalwart off-road prowess and roots dating back to World War II and the original Willys Jeep. After the war, the Civilian Jeep (CJ) was produced from the mid-1940s through 1986, first by Willys, then by Kaiser-Jeep and American Motors Corporation (AMC), then, when Chrysler purchased AMC in 1987, it created the first Jeep Wrangler with a lot of AMC-produced parts. In fact, the last AMC-developed engine wasn't discontinued until 2012. Today's Jeep Wrangler is a picture of modernity with power windows, navigation systems, premium audio, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, heated front seats, front and side airbags, and push-button start. But the design perpetually harks back to an earlier time, with the classic seven-slot grille and the option to ditch the windshield and the doors. Jeep Wrangler: Cost, Reliability, and the Best Years to Buy Frequently Asked Questions Jeep Wrangler Pros and Cons Jeep Wrangler Generations Jeep Wrangler Fourth Generation (2019–Present) Jeep Wrangler Third Generation (2007–2018) Jeep Wrangler Second Generation (1997–2006) Jeep Wrangler First Generation (1986–1995) Frequently Asked Questions Which Jeep Wrangler years are the best? If you look at CarComplaints.com, the second generation and current generation of the Jeep Wrangler seem to have the fewest problems and complaints. Consumer Reports generally shows poor predictive reliability across the board, but the last couple of years have been trending upwards. So, we'd say newer is probably better — especially if the factory warranty is still valid. What are the worst Jeep Wrangler years? The third-generation Jeep Wrangler logs the most problems on CarComplaints.com, with the 2007 model being known for the "death wobble" — sudden and uncontrollable movement of the front suspension, which is very apparent through the steering wheel — and 2008 logging the most complaints of any other model year. However, the website dubs 2012 the worst model year due to electrical problems. How much does a late-model Jeep Wrangler cost? Late-model Jeep Wranglers hold their value well, so expect to pay a premium for a recent one. On CarGurus, a 1-year-old 2025 Wrangler lists for around $37,400, while a 3-year-old 2023 model averages roughly $35,500. Step down to a 5-year-old 2021 Wrangler and the average drops to about $29,400, giving you the most room to save while staying close to the current generation. Research Jeep Wrangler Price Trends on CarGurus Is a used Jeep Wrangler a good deal? If you're willing to take a risk on a vehicle known for reliability issues, there are plenty of good deals to be had. We see second-generation Wranglers on sale for less than $5,000, and third-gen vehicles priced at less than $10,000. Even examples of the most recent fourth-generation model can be found for less than $15,000. Jeep Wrangler Pros and Cons Pros: Unparalleled off-road chops Removable top and doors Highly customizable Cons: Poor ride quality on tarmac Excessive wind noise at highway speeds Less cargo volume than other SUVs Jeep Wrangler Generations Jeep Wrangler Fourth Generation (2019–Present) The fourth-generation Jeep Wrangler — referred to by the manufacturer as the Wrangler JL — looks remarkably similar to its predecessors, but it received significant upgrades. It's longer and wider, for better accessibility, plus it offers new and updated engines, an easier-to-fold windshield, easier-to-remove doors, an optional Sky One-Touch Power Top, zipperless soft tops, blind-spot monitoring, improved off-road capability, and better on-road performance. This new Jeep generation retained the standard 3.6-liter Pentastar V6 engine and added a 270-horsepower, 2.0-liter turbo four-cylinder engine, which is available with all trims. A six-speed manual transmission is standard with the V6, while an eight-speed automatic is optional with the V6 and standard with the four-cylinder engine. A 260-horsepower 3.0-liter turbocharged EcoDiesel engine was available from 2020 to 2023 and in 2021, Jeep introduced a Hemi V8-powered version of the Rubicon trim level, called the Rubicon 392, which delivered 470 horsepower and 470 pound-feet of torque. The Rubicon 392 was replaced with the Wrangler 392 Final Edition in 2025, though the 6.4-liter Hemi V8 returns for 2026 in the new Moab 392 special edition. This generation also saw the debut of the first electrified version in 2021: the Jeep Wrangler 4xe with a plug-in hybrid drivetrain. The interior may look retro but it's thoroughly modern, with push-button start as standard and an available digital gauge cluster, and all models can be equipped with heated front seats and a heated steering wheel. The fourth-gen Wrangler uses the Uconnect infotainment system across the board, but depending on trim is available in five, seven, or 8.4-inch displays. In terms of safety, the Wrangler JL adds standard side-impact airbags, available driver-assist features, and a lower beltline to increase visibility out of the windows. However, the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety has found this generation has the propensity to overturn during the small front overlap crash test and gives it a marginal score for this metric. Changes throughout this generation have included the addition of optional adaptive cruise control in 2019 and an Xtreme Recon package with 35-inch all-terrain tires and suspension lift in 2021. The JL got a mid-cycle refresh in 2024, which included new tire and wheel combinations, a different grille design, a new Rubicon X trim, updated Uconnect, a standard 12.3-inch infotainment screen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, and a redesigned center stack. For 2026, Jeep is producing 12 special edition Wranglers, dubbed the Twelve 4 Twelve, in celebration of 85 years of off-road leadership. The first edition, Moab 392, focuses on performance enhancements. Sporting the 6.4-liter V8, the Moab 392 is loaded with dedicated off-road hardware, including 17-inch beadlock-capable wheels fitted with 35-inch all-terrain tires, rock protection sill rails, and a cold-air intake hood. The second edition, Whitecap, is more of an appearance package that adds to the Sahara or Rubicon trim, offering a bright white special edition paint color and side stripe detail, heated Nappa leather seats, and an Alpine audio system. Other 2026 updates include revised door hinges that make the doors easier to remove, newly available steel bumpers, a Warn winch on the two-door Willys, and a refreshed color palette. The MSRP for the 2026 Wrangler Sport starts at $34,895 for the two-door including a $1,995 destination fee, with four-door versions adding roughly $4,000 to $5,000, but that price can jump up quickly for higher trim levels or the plug-in hybrid powertrain. The special edition Moab 392 starts at $79,995 including destination. If you're trying to snag one of the last Hemi models, those will cost you at least $100,590 before destination. On the used market, the earliest model years of this generation average just shy of $25,000, while the latest model years average around $37,400. For more information, read our full guide to Jeep Wrangler Engine Longevity . Jeep Wrangler Third Generation (2007–2018) The third-generation Jeep Wrangler was the first clean-sheet design of the body, frame, and suspension. Known as the JK, these Wrangler models added features such as power windows, remote power door locks, a navigation system, and available detachable sway bars. In addition to the traditional two-door models, a standard four-door Unlimited version was permanently added to the lineup. However, unlike the TJ-based Unlimited model, the wheelbase was 20 inches longer rather than 10 inches. Stability control was a new safety feature offered on the JK Wrangler, and all trims had off-road-tuned anti-lock brakes and traction control with an electronic limited-slip differential. The Rubicon was standard with an electronic sway bar disconnect system. The Sunrider convertible soft top was standard, and an optional three-piece modular hardtop was available. Though some luxury amenities were added and most functions were under computer software control, the Wrangler JK still had a separate body-on-frame chassis, rigid live axles, a fold-flat windshield, and the ability to be driven without doors. The 4X4 models also still had part-time four-wheel drive with high and low gearing. The third-generation Jeep Wrangler also had a wider track and was available with bigger tires. The two-door model was 2.5 inches shorter than the previous generation, and the Unlimited four-door model was 14 inches longer than the TJ Unlimited. The initial powertrain in the JK Jeep Wrangler was the 202-hp 3.8-liter V6, paired with a base six-speed manual or an optional four-speed automatic transmission. It was offered through 2011, when it was replaced by the 285-hp, Chrysler 3.6-liter Pentastar V6, which retained the same six-speed manual transmission, but the automatic was upgraded to a five-speed. Hill Start Assist was added in 2009, and 2010 brought an easier-to-fold soft top. DaimlerChrysler's Uconnect touchscreen infotainment system became standard on models with the MyGig radio at that time. A mid-cycle refresh arrived in 2011, with a redesigned interior, Bluetooth connectivity, cruise control, optional Garmin-based navigation, SiriusXM Satellite Radio, available heated front seats, and new aluminum alloy wheel options. Small changes occurred throughout the rest of this generation's run, including a one-handed rear-folding seat and ambient lighting in 2013, clear park lights in 2014, a new 552-watt Alpine premium audio system in 2015, and 75th Anniversary and Golden Eagle editions for 2018. Even with some of the problems in this generation (such as the aforementioned death wobble), used prices remain high, but there is a lot of availability and deals can be found if you're willing to travel for them. We've seen some Jeep Wranglers in this generation priced as low as $4,000, but we've also seen heavily modified Jeeps in the $100,000 range. However, you should be able to find a good third-gen Wrangler with lower miles and zero accidents in the $10,000 to $15,000 bracket. Jeep Wrangler Second Generation (1997–2006) Though the second-gen Jeep Wrangler was introduced in early 1996, it was positioned as a 1997 model, and Jeep skipped the 1996 model year. Known as the TJ, this generation reintroduced the round headlamps from the classic Jeeps and, instead of leaf springs, this generation used coil-spring suspension for better ride and handling. Initially, it was available in SE, Sport, and Sahara trim levels. Other changes included dual front airbags, optional anti-lock brakes, integrated air vents, the addition of a glove box, and car-like stereo controls. The 2.5-liter inline-four and 4.0-liter inline-six engines were carried over from the previous generation, as were the three-speed automatic and five-speed manual transmissions. In 2003, however, Jeep ditched the 2.5-liter engine in favor of a 147-hp, 2.4-liter four-cylinder engine, previously used in the Chrysler PT Cruiser. At the same time, the three-speed automatic was replaced by a four-speed equivalent and, in 2005, the five-speed manual was swapped for a six-speeder. The Jeep Wrangler Rubicon model, named for the Rubicon Trail, was added in 2002, featuring rear air-actuated locking Dana 44 axles with the Rock-Trac NV241 4:1 ratio transfer case, 16-inch alloy wheels, and Goodyear MTR P245/75-R16 tires. The Jeep Wrangler Unlimited arrived in 2004, with a 10-inch longer wheelbase, which added a standard Dana 44 rear axle with a 3.73 gear ratio and the Command-Trac NV231 transfer case. A mid-cycle refresh in 2003 brought new wheel designs and exterior decals, the new 2.4-liter engine, a new steering wheel, revised interior switch gear, new audio systems, Sirius Satellite Radio, and redesigned seats. The last model year of the Wrangler TJ brought the 65th Anniversary Edition and the Golden Eagle Edition, plus the four-cylinder engine was dropped and the 4.0-liter inline six became standard. Prices for a second-generation Wrangler range from about $6,000 for an accident-damaged example to about $23,000 for one with low miles and no accidents. The average is around $12,000. Jeep Wrangler First Generation (1986–1995) The first official Jeep Wrangler appeared under the Chrysler umbrella after the Civilian Jeep (CJ) series was discontinued. Internally known as the Wrangler YJ, the first-generation Wrangler distinguished itself from its predecessor by its square headlights, but it rode on the same wheelbase. Though the grille was new, the body was still very similar to the old CJs, while several parts were interchangeable. In an attempt to attract more daily drivers, the first-gen Wrangler got a wider track than the CJ, had less ground clearance, more comfort, and improved handling. It also got trackbar suspension links and anti-roll bars for improved safety, which made it harder to flip. The base engine in the first-gen Jeep Wrangler was a 117-horsepower, 2.5-liter inline four cylinder, while a larger 112-hp 4.2-liter inline six was available — both developed by AMC. A five-speed manual transmission was standard, and a three-speed automatic was an option with the inline six. In 1988, Jeep introduced the high-end Wrangler Sahara model and, in 1991, a fuel-injected 190-horsepower, 4.0-liter straight-six engine replaced the original inline six. The roll cage was extended in 1992, which allowed for rear shoulder belts, and anti-lock brakes were added as an option in 1993. Then, in 1994, the four-cylinder engines gained a three-speed automatic as an option. There are still quite a few first-gen Jeep Wranglers in circulation, and we saw everything from salvage vehicles for less than $1,000 to low-mileage Wranglers in excellent condition for around $40,000, but most of the vehicles for sale in this generation were in the $5,000 to $10,000 ballpark. title: Why AML Investigators Need AI
summary: Maya logs in to find 47 alerts. Her queue grew by eight since Friday, and it's only Tuesday. Here's what changes when an AI investigator works alongside her.
body_text: Maya has been an AML analyst for three years. She works at a mid-sized fintech that processes about $2B annually, serving small businesses across the U.S. The work matters. Most days feel like treading water. This morning, she logs into the case management system and sees 47 alerts in her queue. Yesterday she closed five cases. The day before, four. Her queue has grown by eight since Friday, and it's only Tuesday. The alert She clicks into the next case. A small business account with a pattern of round-dollar wire transfers totaling $127,000 over six weeks. Funds went to three Delaware LLCs registered within the past 90 days. The account holder runs a landscaping company in Ohio. On the surface, it could be anything. A renovation. A scam victim. Or something worse. Maya has seen all of it. Investigating manually She opens a blank Notes doc. The case management system is clunky, so she's learned to keep her own record. She pulls six months of transactions, scans for patterns, and starts cross-referencing. She pulls KYC, runs OFAC, checks adverse media, and follows the registered-agent thread into a rabbit hole of related LLCs. Eight tabs deep, four-page Notes doc. Ninety minutes in, her queue has grown by two more alerts. Investigating with Roe Now imagine a different morning. Maya arrives at 8:30 AM. The 47 alerts are still there, but 43 of them already have completed investigation summaries waiting for her review. Roe worked through the queue overnight. Within seconds of an alert landing, Roe forms an investigation plan from your SOPs. It pulls transactions, queries public records, runs sanctions, searches the web, and reviews prior alerts. It iterates: a query reveals a registered-agent network, so it follows the thread. On average: 8–15 iterations and 100–250 steps per case, ~15 minutes per investigation. What Maya sees Maya opens the case. The first thing she sees is the recommended action: suspected suspicious activity. Each finding links to its evidence: ‘Recipient LLCs registered within 90 days’ links to the Delaware records. ‘Round-dollar transfers totaling $127,000’ links to the transactions. ‘Registered agent associated with 14 other LLCs’ links to the public records search. If she wants to go deeper, she can. She drills into the full investigation log: every query, every search, every decision point. Maya is not asked to blindly trust an AI recommendation. She is given a verifiable evidence package. The feedback loop Maya agrees with the conclusion: a money mule, likely a victim of a job scam. But the velocity threshold flagged feels too sensitive for small businesses. She adjusts it. Future investigations calibrate. Later, another case uses a signal she hadn't seen: a mail-drop database check. She decides it's valuable and adds it to the SOP. The system learns from her, and she learns from it. What this means for investigators AI does not replace Maya. It handles data gathering, pattern recognition, and tedious cross-referencing across a dozen sources. Maya makes the final call. The work is still demanding. The balance shifts.

title: In Conversation with mendezmendez
summary: Digital collage artist mendezmendez on his daily creative practice, surrealism influences, and using AI as source material.
body_text: mendezmendez has been making digital collage since 2009, spending the first year and a half creating purely for himself before the work found its audience. Building on years of prior experimentation with vector illustration, digital painting, and other techniques, he discovered in digital collage something that none of those other mediums offered: an improvisational freedom that let random elements collide into unexpected meaning. Influenced by the surrealism of Magritte, the mathematical precision of Escher, and the pioneering digital collage work of Eduardo Recife, he developed a practice rooted in curiosity and a willingness to pull from anywhere, public domain paintings, Hubble telescope imagery, vintage biology illustrations, AI-generated figures, and his own sketches. His latest drop, ENTROPY , a body of work composed of three interconnected series (Combustion, Corruption, and Diffusion), is available to mint July 30 using OpenSea. In early 2024, a 28-day creative challenge broke him out of a creative block and transformed his entire approach. What began as a short sprint became a permanent daily practice, and in the two and a half years since, he has produced over 840 works. That relentless output has sharpened a signature style, spawned multiple series, and opened doors he hadn't anticipated. We sat down with mendezmendez to talk about the discipline behind the daily work, his medium-agnostic approach to source material, and where he sees digital collage heading next. Process Trad Digital Collage. Image courtesy of artist. OpenSea: You've been making digital collage since 2009, that's well over a decade of self-teaching. What did those early years look like, and how did you know you were onto something worth sticking with? mendezmendez: Prior to the start of my digital collage practice in 2009, I was already making digital art and design for five years or so. During those first years, I experimented with vector illustration, mixing pencil drawings with digital painting, 3D, compositing, and other techniques. So when I began experimenting with digital collage, the foundational skills needed to create the work were there. It became obvious to me that this would become my preferred medium because from the very first piece I created, I fell in love with the improvisational nature of the collage process. Being able to throw seemingly random elements onto a canvas, play with their arrangement, discover novel ways in which they could interact, and uncover new meaning through those relationships was incredibly inspiring. I was hooked. I spent about a year and a half creating collages just for myself, and surprisingly, those early works still hold up to this day. OpenSea: The name "mendezmendez" is pretty distinctive. Where did it come from, and how do you think about the online persona you've built around it? mendezmendez: I wish there was a more interesting story behind it, but the reality is that Mendez Mendez is simply my real last name. The repetition is just a coincidence since both my parents share the same surname. Honestly, there has never been some grand strategy behind building a brand or community. It has all happened naturally through simply showing up every day and remaining consistent with my work. The process. Image courtesy of artist. OpenSea: Your influences span centuries and styles, from Escher's geometry to Magritte's surrealism to Eduardo Recife's digital collage roots. How do those references actually show up in your process? Is it conscious, or more like something that sneaks into the work? mendezmendez: After so many years and well over a thousand artworks created, these references still influence me, but mostly on a subconscious level. Eduardo Recife was my main stylistic reference when I first began. He is a master of the classic digital collage aesthetic. From Magritte, I have quite shamelessly appropriated the sky textured human form. He is my favorite surrealist because of his blend of minimalism and surrealism, executed with such clean and precise painting. Escher, on the other hand, was as much a mathematician and scientist as he was an artist. I have always been fascinated by the relationship between science and art, particularly through optical illusions, and in my opinion, M.C. Escher is one of the greatest examples of that intersection. OpenSea: In early 2024, you made a pretty significant shift from perfectionism to a daily creation practice. What pushed you to make that change, and what did you have to let go of to get there? mendezmendez: Originally, I set out to create a new piece every day for twenty eight days with a few friends as part of a creative challenge. I was experiencing a creative block at the time, so I figured a challenge like this would help pull me out of that funk. About two weeks into it, I experienced a complete paradigm shift in how I approached the creative process and in my assumptions about what was possible to create in a single session. Doors and opportunities began to open simply from sharing these daily works, and I saw that as proof of concept for what a daily practice could mean for my career. When the twenty eight day challenge ended, there was absolutely no doubt in my mind that I would continue creating daily works for as long as I am physically and mentally able. To this day, I have created over 840 artworks in two and a half years. Through this process, I have developed a signature style, new techniques, multiple series, and major projects. A friend who has been observing my trajectory told me it feels like I have been speed running through my art career since beginning this daily practice. My only regret is not having started sooner. 2010. Image courtesy of artist. OpenSea: Your source material comes from a pretty wide net, including Public Domain paintings, photography, 3D renders, AI, and your own sketches. How do you decide what a piece needs? Is there a moment where you just know the right element when you see it? mendezmendez: I am completely medium agnostic when it comes to source material. Certain elements are simply better when sourced from their original mediums. For example, if I want to displace a human form with ripple textures, I will specifically seek out water ripple photography. If I need flora or fauna, I often source those from vintage biology illustration books. Marbled paper textures always come from public domain sources. I use AI to generate human forms in very specific poses and angles. I prefer AI over 3D for this because of how quickly I can create a posed human form with an oil painting texture. With 3D, the process often feels too slow, rigid, and cold for my workflow. I am far too accustomed to the fast paced nature of digital collage to spend hours posing, texturing, and rendering a figure. My signature clouds come from an 1800s painting, while my stars are sourced from Hubble telescope imagery. At the end of the day, I will use anything and everything necessary to materialize an idea. OpenSea: Surrealism has a long history, but digital collage as a medium is still relatively young. Where do you think the form is headed, and what do you feel you're contributing to it? mendezmendez: The term "surrealism" gets used very loosely, especially in digital collage, but I think it is often misapplied to describe abstract collage compositions. True surrealism must maintain a foundation in realism, then disrupt that realism with something impossible. For a while, I felt that much of the digital collage I was seeing online was beginning to look too similar. This was largely due to artists relying on the same limited pool of public domain source material available from museums and libraries. Once I began noticing this pattern, I felt compelled to expand my source material, which is what led me to incorporate 3D and AI into my practice. I believe digital collage will continue evolving into a broader mixed digital media form, breaking free from the traditional retro and vintage aesthetic that has long defined public domain collage work. I would love to think that my own approach might inspire other collage artists to embrace AI simply as another source material within their workflow, because it offers artists the opportunity to develop a far more unique visual language that helps them stand apart stylistically. 2009. Image courtesy of artist. OpenSea: Consistency is something you talk about openly, showing up every day and trusting the process even when a piece doesn't land. Has that discipline changed the way you relate to your own work, or how you measure what a "successful" piece even is? mendezmendez: You would think that after more than 840 artworks, I would have a stronger grasp on what makes a piece successful, but honestly, I don’t. The cliché that "art is subjective" is very real, and that reality only becomes more apparent at scale. Every single day I share a new piece, I genuinely have no idea how people will respond to it. Whenever a piece unexpectedly resonates and reaches hundreds of thousands of people, it always comes as a surprise. I use that uncertainty as motivation to stay focused on what personally interests me. I have always made art for myself first. Whether others connect with it or not is ultimately outside of my control. So yes, this discipline has absolutely changed my perspective. It has reinforced the importance of focusing on creating what I find meaningful, because I cannot control audience preferences. Even if I could predict what others wanted, I would never compromise my integrity as an artist simply to cater to external expectations. OpenSea: What's next for mendezmendez? Are there any new projects or upcoming releases you can share with us? mendezmendez: The daily practice will continue indefinitely. It is the foundation of my creative process now and the core mechanism through which I develop new bodies of work. Beyond that, I am currently working on a continuation of my animated impressionist series, but with an entirely different approach in process from the first iteration. I am also deeply engaged in building my own software tools for experimental art series, as well as exploring autonomous art systems, plotter based works, and generative art. It’s an incredible time to be a digital artist! Honestly, I am having a ridiculous amount of fun in the studio lately, and I am hopeful that all of this experimentation will lead to new series that are worthy of sharing with the world. ‍Disclaimer: This content is for informational purposes only and should not be construed as financial or trading advice. summary: Build a branded notification preference center with no code. Let users control what they get, preview before you publish, and launch on web and mobile.
body_text: A notification preference center is where your users decide what they hear from you, on which channels, and how often. Get it right and people mute the one topic that's bugging them instead of unsubscribing from everything. The catch is that building one is a real project, and keeping it branded and responsive across every device is more work still. We've made it much easier. Courier's redesigned preference tooling lets you build a preference center in a visual editor, preview it before anyone sees it, and give users a page that looks great on web and mobile, with no frontend code. Configure topics, sections, and branding on the left. Preview the live page on the right, on desktop or mobile. Design your preference center in a redesigned editor The Preferences Editor is where you decide what users can control. We rebuilt it to be quicker to work in, with a live preview so you see exactly what users will get before you publish. The whole page is yours to shape: Subscription topics users opt in or out of, like Marketing or Account Activity, grouped into sections . Branding and wording , from your logo and colors to the heading, description, and channel names, so the page reads in your product's voice. Default states per topic: on, off, or required for the notifications users can't turn off. Digests , now simple to set up. Add delivery schedules like daily or weekly in a few clicks, and let users batch a noisy topic into one summary instead of a stream of individual messages. Channel selection , so users choose which channels deliver each topic, across any channel you send on, from email and SMS to push, chat, and more. Preview before you publish Your changes save as a draft and never reach users until you publish. Hit Preview Page to see the preference center exactly as a user will, marked with a "Draft mode" banner, then Publish when it's right. No more guessing what an edit will look like, and no more pushing changes straight to live users. A hosted preference center, no code required Courier hosts this page for you, so there's nothing to build, deploy, or maintain. The hosted preference center, matched to your brand. Users toggle topics on or off and pick a digest schedule, like daily or weekly. The page picks up your brand automatically. Your logo, colors, and typography carry over, so it looks like part of your product instead of a bolt-on, and it follows along when you change your brand. It's responsive, so it looks right on everything from a laptop to a phone without you touching any CSS. And one-click unsubscribe is built in, so you stay compliant without building opt-out flows yourself. Start with the hosted page, customize later Many teams start with the hosted page to launch in an afternoon, then build a fully custom experience once they know exactly what they want. You can embed the same preferences directly in your own product, with prebuilt components for web (React, web components) and mobile (iOS, Android, React Native, Flutter), and take full control of the layout and styling. It's the same preference data underneath, so moving from hosted to embedded is a step forward, not a rebuild. Migrate preferences in bulk New bulk API endpoints update all of a user's preferences in a single request. Importing your existing subscription and opt-out data from another system becomes one call per user, instead of setting topics one at a time. Replace a user's entire set at once , or update only the topics you name . Try it Open the Preferences Editor to set up your topics, or read the preferences overview to see how it all fits together. Frequently asked questions What is a notification preference center? A page where your users manage which notifications they receive from your product, on which channels, and how often. It usually covers subscription topics they can opt in or out of, channel choices, digest frequency, and one-click unsubscribe. Do I need developers to set one up? No. You configure and brand the whole page in the visual Preferences Editor and link to the hosted version, with no frontend code. Developers can step in later to embed a custom version or manage preferences over the API. What's the difference between a hosted and embedded preference center? A hosted preference center is a page Courier hosts and you link to, with no frontend code. Embedded preferences render inside your own web or mobile app with prebuilt components, for full control over layout and styling. Both read and write the same preference data, so you can start hosted and move to embedded later without a rebuild. Can users choose how often they get notified? Yes. Turn on digests for a topic and users pick a schedule, like instant, daily, or weekly, so a busy topic arrives as one summary instead of a stream of messages. How do users unsubscribe? Every subscription topic includes one-click unsubscribe, and you can add an unsubscribe link to any notification. Because users opt out of a single topic rather than all of your messages, you keep more of them subscribed overall. Can I match the preference center to my brand? Yes. The hosted page uses your brand automatically for its logo, colors, and typography, and it's responsive on web and mobile out of the box. How do I move existing preferences into Courier? Use the bulk API to set all of a user's preferences in one request. You can import your existing subscription and opt-out data one user at a time, without rebuilding it topic by topic.

title: Agent Offboarding and Decommissioning
summary: Agentic Fabriq is the identity and permissioning layer for AI agents. Per-agent identity, least-privilege access, full audit logs, and one-click revocation across MCP, OAuth, and agent frameworks. Drop-in with Okta, Azure AD, and Google Workspace.
body_text: Overview Agent offboarding is one of the most overlooked parts of enterprise AI governance. It is the final stage of the agent lifecycle—and the one that almost no one plans for. Teams pour energy into proposing, approving, and launching agents. Far fewer think carefully about how to retire them. But every agent eventually reaches the end of its useful life. A project wraps up. A workflow is redesigned. A newer, better agent replaces an older one. A vendor relationship ends. The person who owned the agent leaves the company. An experiment quietly fails. A permission that once made sense is no longer needed. When that moment arrives, the agent should be decommissioned properly —not simply abandoned. Offboarding is the discipline of removing an agent from operation completely and verifiably, so that nothing it once held remains active. This post lays out what a clean decommissioning process looks like, and why the absence of one is a security problem hiding in plain sight. Why It Gets Skipped Offboarding is skipped for the same reasons it is dangerous. An agent that is no longer used generates no complaints. No one files a ticket because an agent stopped being invoked. The workflow simply moves on, and the agent fades from attention while quietly retaining everything it was granted. There is also a structural reason. Provisioning has a clear owner and a clear moment: someone wants the agent, so someone builds it. Decommissioning has neither by default. The person who would benefit from retiring an agent cleanly is rarely the person who notices it is idle. Without an explicit process, the work has no home—and work with no home does not get done. The result is accumulation. Every team that has deployed agents for more than a year tends to discover a backlog of forgotten ones: a marketing campaign agent still holding write access to the ad platform, a data pipeline agent whose service account never expired, a procurement assistant tied to a vendor the company stopped using months ago. When Offboarding Begins Offboarding should not depend on someone remembering. The triggers that should start a decommissioning process are predictable, and most of them already produce signals elsewhere in the enterprise: The agent is replaced. A newer agent takes over the same workflow, leaving the old one redundant. The workflow changes. The business process the agent supported has been redesigned or eliminated. The owner leaves. The business or technical owner departs, and no one inherits the agent—a strong signal it should be reviewed for retirement. The vendor or integration is removed. A SaaS platform or third-party service the agent depended on is no longer in use. The experiment ends. A pilot or proof-of-concept concludes without graduating to production. The agent goes idle. Usage drops to zero for a sustained period, suggesting its purpose has quietly disappeared. A mature program wires these triggers into its agent inventory. When an owner is offboarded from the HR system, the agents they owned should surface for review. When an integration is decommissioned, the agents that used it should be flagged automatically. The Decommissioning Sequence Proper decommissioning is a sequence, not a single action. Each step closes off a different way the agent could remain a liability after it is supposed to be gone. The order matters: you announce the change before you break things, and you confirm access is gone before you consider the agent retired. 1. Mark as Deprecated or Retired The first step is to change the agent's status in the agent inventory or registry. Marking it deprecated and then retired creates a clear, durable record that it is no longer approved to operate. This matters because the inventory is the source of truth for what should exist. An agent that still appears as active after it has been turned off creates ambiguity—and ambiguity is exactly what lets stale access survive. A status change also gives every downstream review, audit, and access check a single signal to act on. # Registry record after decommissioning agent_id: fin-close-reconciler-02 status: retired retired_on: 2026-07-08 retired_by: paulina@agenticfabriq.com reason: replaced by fin-close-reconciler-03 permissions: revoked credentials: revoked schedules: stopped logs: retained (policy: finance-7y) 2. Notify Dependents If anyone depends on the agent, they should be told before it disappears. An agent that supports a live business workflow cannot simply be switched off without warning—teams may need migration time, or a window to validate that a replacement behaves correctly. Consider a quarterly close reconciliation agent used by the finance team. Even if a newer agent is ready, finance needs to confirm the new one produces matching results before the old one is removed. Notification turns a disruptive surprise into a planned cutover. It also surfaces hidden dependencies you didn't know existed—someone always replies that their report quietly relies on the agent you thought no one used. 3. Remove Permissions Once dependents are handled, the agent's permissions should be removed. This is the heart of offboarding, because permissions are what made the agent powerful in the first place. Retiring an agent while leaving its access in place removes the convenience but keeps the risk. Permission removal has to be exhaustive. Agents accumulate access across many surfaces, and any one that is missed becomes a residual exposure: SaaS application scopes and connected-app grants API access to internal and external services Database roles and query permissions Document and file-store access Source code repositories and CI systems Chat and collaboration system memberships Ticketing and workflow tool access Internal service-to-service authorizations This is where an action-level inventory earns its keep. If you know precisely what an agent was authorized to do, you know precisely what to revoke—and you can confirm afterward that nothing was left behind. 4. Revoke Credentials Removing permissions and revoking credentials are not the same thing, and both are required. Permissions define what the agent is allowed to do; credentials are the keys it holds . A credential that is still valid can sometimes reach systems whose access controls were configured loosely, so leaving keys live is its own distinct risk. Every credential the agent was ever issued should be invalidated: OAuth tokens and refresh tokens API keys Service account credentials Secrets stored in vaults or configuration Delegated access granted on behalf of users Delegated access deserves special attention. A legal review agent that operated on behalf of individual attorneys may hold tokens scoped to their identities. Those delegations must be unwound explicitly, or the retired agent could still act as someone else long after it is supposedly gone. 5. Stop Scheduled Jobs and Automations An agent can keep running long after people stop invoking it manually. Scheduled jobs, event triggers, webhooks, and recurring automations all execute on their own. Decommissioning has to reach these mechanisms directly. Imagine an IT operations agent that was set up to run a nightly log-cleanup routine. Users stopped interacting with it months ago, but the cron trigger never knew that. Every night it still wakes up, authenticates, and acts on production systems. Until the schedule itself is disabled, "no one uses it anymore" is simply not true. Always confirm that the agent is no longer firing on any timer or event after you believe it is retired. 6. Retain Logs According to Policy Retiring an agent does not mean erasing the record of what it did. Decommissioning removes the agent's ability to act ; it should not remove the evidence of its past actions . Audit trails, action logs, and approval records should be retained according to your retention policy—which is often dictated by compliance requirements rather than convenience. If a sales forecasting agent made decisions that affected reported pipeline, you may need to reconstruct exactly what it did, months later, even though the agent itself no longer exists. Decommissioning the actor and preserving the history are complementary, not contradictory. 7. Update Ownership Records Finally, ownership records should reflect the new reality. If the agent was retired outright, the inventory should show who retired it and why. If it was replaced, the replacement should be registered, reviewed, and assigned its own owner before the old one is fully removed. This closes the loop with the rest of the lifecycle. A retirement that updates ownership keeps the inventory honest; a retirement that doesn't leaves orphaned records that look real but point to nothing. The handoff between a retired agent and its successor is also the natural moment to confirm that the new agent inherited only the access it actually needs—not a copy of everything the old one had. The Invisible Access Path The risk of poor offboarding is simple to state: abandoned agents become invisible access paths into enterprise systems. They retain permissions long after their purpose disappears. They hold stale credentials that no one is watching. They have no current owner to notice if something goes wrong. And they may continue to run in the background on their own schedule. Each of these is a problem on its own; together, they describe an entry point that is powerful, unmonitored, and not on anyone's list. These are precisely the conditions attackers look for. An agent identity with live credentials, broad access, and no accountable owner is more attractive than a forgotten human account, because it was designed to act autonomously and is expected to. The danger is not that the agent does anything malicious—it is that the access it carries outlives the oversight that justified it. An abandoned agent is not a harmless leftover. It is a credentialed, capable actor that no one is governing—exactly the kind of access path you would never approve if someone proposed it on purpose. In Practice Making offboarding real means turning it from a hope into a routine. A few practices make the difference between a policy that exists on paper and one that actually closes access: • Tie decommissioning to existing triggers. When an owner leaves through HR, when a vendor contract ends in procurement, or when an integration is removed in IT, let those events automatically flag the affected agents for review. • Detect idleness automatically. Agents with no activity for a defined window should surface in a review queue rather than waiting to be remembered. • Make the sequence a checklist, not a memory. Status, notification, permissions, credentials, automations, logs, ownership—each item verified, not assumed. • Verify after the fact. After retiring an agent, confirm that its credentials no longer authenticate and its schedules no longer fire. Removal is not complete until it is confirmed. If Agents Can Be Provisioned, They Must Be Deprovisioned A mature Agent Operations program treats offboarding as seriously as onboarding. The same rigor that governs how an agent enters production should govern how it leaves it—because the access an agent carries does not disappear on its own. Provisioning and decommissioning are two halves of the same discipline. One grants identity, scope, and credentials; the other reclaims them. A program that does only the first accumulates risk with every agent it launches. A program that does both keeps its agent landscape honest: what exists is approved, what is approved is owned, and what is retired is truly gone. If agents can be provisioned, they must also be deprovisioned. Clean retirement is not the unglamorous end of the lifecycle—it is what keeps the rest of your governance true.

title: The best Clearbit alternatives in 2026
summary: Clearbit is gone as a standalone product, now Breeze Intelligence inside HubSpot. Here are the best Clearbit alternatives in 2026 for enrichment and visitor reveal.
body_text: Clearbit no longer exists as a standalone product. HubSpot acquired it in December 2023 and sunset it through 2025; its capabilities now live inside HubSpot as Breeze Intelligence. If you relied on Clearbit for enrichment, form shortening, or Reveal's visitor identification, you need a replacement. Here are the best options in 2026. Clearbit did three jobs: enrich records with firmographic and contact data, shorten forms with autofill, and reveal which companies visited your site. Those jobs are now split across different tools, or bundled into HubSpot if you live there. The right alternative depends on which of the three mattered most to you, and whether you want the data to sit in a dashboard or actually drive outreach. Comparison table Rank Tool Best for Standout capability Public pricing 1 Artisan Teams that want data and visitor reveal to trigger automated outreach Enrichment plus person and company identification feeding Ava's autonomous campaigns Usage-based credits for Ava's work; dialer seats billed separately; free trial ( pricing ) 2 HubSpot Breeze Intelligence Teams fully committed to HubSpot Clearbit's successor, native to HubSpot Credits inside HubSpot (per HubSpot pricing) 3 Clay GTM teams with an operator to run enrichment Over 150 providers, Claygent agents, waterfall enrichment $167-446/month public tiers 4 Apollo Budget-conscious teams wanting data plus basic outreach Over 230M contacts in an all-in-one Free to $119/user/month 5 ZoomInfo Enterprises that need deep US data Largest verified US B2B data graph Over $15K/year entry (buyer-reported) 6 Vector Teams replacing Clearbit Reveal specifically Person and contact-level visitor intent $399-999/month, month-to-month How we chose We split Clearbit's job into its parts and asked which alternative rebuilds each best. Data quality and coverage against realistic benchmarks. Whether visitor reveal is included and at what depth. Pricing transparency, since Clearbit's opacity was a common complaint. And, for buyers weighing this post-acquisition, whether the tool does anything with the data or just stores it. Enrichment is a means to an end. What are the best Clearbit alternatives? They divide by which Clearbit feature you are replacing. For enrichment, Clay (orchestration), Apollo (all-in-one value), and ZoomInfo (enterprise depth). For Reveal's visitor identification, Vector (person-level) and Artisan (person plus company, with outreach attached). For HubSpot-native teams, Breeze Intelligence is the official continuation. Only one of these treats the data as a trigger for action instead of a destination. For the wider market, see the best B2B data providers and the best email and phone number finder tools for sales . 1. Artisan: Data and reveal that become automated outreach Artisan is the alternative for teams that used Clearbit to find and reveal the right accounts, then wished something would act on them. It runs waterfall enrichment across roughly a dozen providers with verified emails and phone numbers (charged only on success), backed by a database of over 250M B2B professionals in over 200 countries, plus Artisan Local Data with over 250M local businesses. It identifies website visitors at the company level on a 3.7B-IP identity graph with a published 92% accuracy rate, and at the person level on 15-30% of US traffic. That covers the enrichment and the Reveal jobs Clearbit did. Then it does the part Clearbit never did. Ava, the autonomous AI BDR, takes enriched records that match your ideal customer profile (ICP) and runs personalized multichannel outreach across email, social media, and dialer call steps, handles the replies from a knowledge base, and books meetings on the right rep's calendar. Ava Inbound greets and qualifies visitors on your site live. Over 90% of customers run Ava autonomously, with a review-and-approve dial, plain-language escalation rules, and a full audit trail. It is SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, and CCPA compliant. Chain of Events, the team behind the RAISE Summit, sourced over $700K of annual recurring revenue (ARR) in six months with Ava, a 20x return on a $28K annual investment, the kind of outcome an enrichment record sitting in a CRM field will never produce. Best for: teams that want Clearbit's data and reveal value plus an AI employee that acts on it; startup through enterprise, including central ops running Ava for large teams Who should pick something else: teams that purely need an enrichment API to feed their own systems and have no interest in outreach; a data-only tool is cheaper for that narrow job Pricing: usage-based credits for Ava's work, so you pay for the work she performs; dialer seats and phone numbers billed separately; free trial. See artisan.co/pricing 2. HubSpot Breeze Intelligence: The official successor Breeze Intelligence is what Clearbit became. If your company runs on HubSpot, it is the path of least resistance: enrichment and buyer intent native to the CRM you already use, priced in HubSpot credits. The catch is the obvious one. It only exists inside HubSpot, so if you left Clearbit partly because you did not want to be locked into HubSpot's world, this does not solve your problem. Best for: teams fully committed to HubSpot who want Clearbit's data continued natively Who should pick something else: anyone not on HubSpot, or teams that want visitor reveal driving multichannel outreach beyond HubSpot's scope Pricing: credits inside HubSpot, per HubSpot's pricing 3. Clay: Enrichment orchestration for operators Clay is the closest replacement for Clearbit's enrichment if you have someone to run it. It orchestrates over 150 data providers in waterfalls, adds Claygent research agents, and gives you enrichment power Clearbit never matched, at $167-446/month public tiers with a $3.1B valuation behind it (August 2025). The tradeoff is real: Clay is a workbench that still needs a worker. It typically needs a skilled go-to-market (GTM) engineer to build and maintain, which is a cost of its own. For a direct comparison, see Clay vs. Clearbit . Best for: GTM teams with an operator who want deep enrichment orchestration Who should pick something else: teams without a dedicated operator, or teams that want the outreach run for them. Clay gives you the workbench; Artisan gives you the worker Pricing: $167-446/month public tiers, plus the operator to run it 4. Apollo: The accessible all-in-one Apollo replaces Clearbit's data at a fraction of the price and adds basic sequencing. Its database claims over 230M contacts, it is used by over 600,000 companies (over 100,000 paying), and it runs from free to $119/user/month. For a smaller team that wants enrichment and light outreach in one affordable tool, it is a strong pick. Its AI assists a rep instead of acting on its own, and enterprises tend to treat Apollo as a data layer rather than the execution engine. For deeper comparisons, see Apollo vs. Lusha and Apollo vs. Outreach . Best for: budget-conscious teams that want data plus basic outreach in one place Who should pick something else: enterprises that need the deepest verified US data (ZoomInfo), or teams that want fully autonomous outreach (Artisan) Pricing: free to $119/user/month, per its pricing page 5. ZoomInfo: Enterprise data depth If Clearbit was your data backbone and you need the most complete verified US B2B data, ZoomInfo is the enterprise standard. It claims over 321M profiles (a vendor figure), repositioned as a go-to-market intelligence platform, and includes WebSights for visitor reveal. It is a data platform first: execution is an add-on, entry runs roughly $15K/year and up per buyer-reported contracts, and its contract terms have a reputation worth diligencing. Best for: enterprises that need the deepest US data and can absorb the cost and contract Who should pick something else: small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) and mid-market teams on tighter budgets, or teams that want the data to drive automated outreach rather than sit in a platform Pricing: roughly $15K/year entry and up, buyer-reported 6. Vector: Replacing Clearbit Reveal specifically If Clearbit Reveal, the visitor identification piece, was the part you miss, Vector is a focused replacement. It does person-level and contact-level visitor intent at $399-999/month, month-to-month, which is refreshingly flexible next to annual data contracts. It identifies and scores; the outreach is still yours to run. Best for: teams replacing Reveal that want person-level intent on a flexible month-to-month plan Who should pick something else: teams that want reveal plus the outreach handled end to end, or teams that need full enrichment alongside identification Pricing: $399-999/month, month-to-month, per its pricing page What is the best enterprise alternative to Clearbit? Two answers, depending on your priority. If deep US data is the point, ZoomInfo is the enterprise standard, with the caveat that execution is a separate purchase. If you want Clearbit's enrichment and reveal to become an operating outbound engine with governance, Artisan is the stronger enterprise choice: central sales ops runs Ava for large account executive (AE) teams who never log in, with single sign-on (SSO) and SAML on Enterprise plans, role-based access, cross-channel do-not-contact enforcement, a full audit trail, and a forward-deployed strategist plus a dedicated customer success manager (CSM). Breeze Intelligence is enterprise-grade only if your enterprise is a HubSpot shop. Should you just move to HubSpot Breeze Intelligence? Move to Breeze if you are already all-in on HubSpot and Clearbit's data was mostly feeding HubSpot workflows anyway. It is the lowest-friction continuation, and the data lineage is the same. Do not move to Breeze if you are not a HubSpot customer, if you want to stay CRM-agnostic, or if the part of Clearbit you valued was reveal driving outreach, which Breeze does not do on its own. In those cases the acquisition is your prompt to pick a tool that fits how you actually sell. What changed with Clearbit? In short, HubSpot bought Clearbit in December 2023 and folded it into its platform, retiring the standalone product and rebranding the capabilities as Breeze Intelligence through 2025. For HubSpot customers, that is a smooth continuation. For everyone else, it forced a decision, which is why this list exists. The broader market shift is that buyers no longer want enrichment as an endpoint. Data that does not move a deal is overhead, and the tools winning attention are the ones that turn a completed record into outreach automatically. Frequently asked questions Is Clearbit still available? Not as a standalone product. HubSpot acquired Clearbit in December 2023 and sunset it through 2025. Its enrichment and intelligence capabilities now exist as Breeze Intelligence inside HubSpot, priced in HubSpot credits. If you are not a HubSpot customer, you need a separate replacement for enrichment, form data, or visitor reveal. What is the best alternative to Clearbit? It depends on which Clearbit feature you relied on. For enrichment with an operator, Clay; for accessible all-in-one data, Apollo; for enterprise US depth, ZoomInfo; for HubSpot-native continuity, Breeze Intelligence. For teams that want the data and visitor reveal to trigger automated, qualified outreach, Artisan, which rebuilds both jobs and adds the AI BDR on top. What replaced Clearbit Reveal? Clearbit Reveal was company-level visitor identification. Modern replacements go further. Vector does person-level and contact-level intent. Artisan identifies visitors company-level on a 3.7B-IP graph at a published 92% accuracy rate and person-level on 15-30% of US traffic, then runs the outreach and chats with visitors via Ava Inbound. Is Breeze Intelligence the same as Clearbit? It is Clearbit's data and capabilities, rebranded and rebuilt natively inside HubSpot. The lineage is the same, but it is only available within HubSpot, which is the key difference from the old standalone Clearbit that many non-HubSpot teams used. If you left Clearbit to avoid HubSpot lock-in, Breeze does not address that. How much did Clearbit cost, and what do alternatives cost? Clearbit's pricing was famously opaque and quote-based. Alternatives are more transparent: Clay runs $167-446/month, Apollo free to $119/user/month, Vector $399-999/month. ZoomInfo starts around $15K/year per buyer reports. Artisan bills Ava's work as usage-based credits with a free trial, and bills dialer seats and phone numbers separately, so the cost tracks the work performed instead of a seat count. Which alternative runs the outreach as well as the data? Artisan. Apollo adds basic sequencing on top of its data, but the outreach is rep-driven. Artisan is the one where enrichment and visitor reveal feed an autonomous AI BDR that writes, sends, replies, and books, with Ava Inbound handling live website chat, all under governance controls suited to enterprise deployment. The bottom line Clearbit's discontinuation is a fork in the road. If you live in HubSpot, Breeze Intelligence is the easy continuation. If you need pure data, Clay, Apollo, or ZoomInfo cover enrichment by budget and depth. But if the reason you used Clearbit was to find the right accounts and then work them, the modern move is a platform that turns data and visitor reveal into pipeline automatically. See how Artisan does it on the homepage , learn about the AI sales agent that runs the outreach, or see how Artisan compares with a visitor-identification specialist in Artisan vs. Qualified .
